name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38

lead: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is a lab-made peptide added to anti-wrinkle serums and creams. The supplier says it prompts skin to make more collagen and hyaluronic acid.
Most efficacy numbers come from the manufacturer. Independent studies test finished products with many ingredients, so the peptide's own contribution is not separated out.

paras: It is described as a matrikine mimic: a fragment-like signal meant to trigger the skin's matrix-building cells. A palmitoyl fatty chain is attached to help it mix with skin lipids.
A 55-person patch test of one serum containing it reported no irritation. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug, and long-term data specific to the peptide are limited.

trials.title: AI-Personalized Skincare Regimen for Facial Photoaging in Women

lead: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is a synthetic lipopeptide used as a cosmetic anti-wrinkle ingredient. It is sold by Sederma, a subsidiary of Croda, under the trade name Matrixyl Synthe'6, and is described by the supplier as a matrikine mimic, meaning a small signalling fragment intended to prompt the skin to remodel its extracellular matrix [1].

Its marketing rests on the claim that it stimulates production of collagens I, III and IV, fibronectin, hyaluronic acid and laminin-5. The most detailed efficacy figures available come from supplier-described testing (a small double-blind study of 25 women using a 2% cream), as reported in an AI-generated encyclopedia summary; independent peer-reviewed trials of the isolated ingredient were not located [1].

Published human studies that include the peptide test finished serums or moisturizers containing many other active ingredients, so effects cannot be attributed to the peptide alone [2][3][4]. It is a cosmetic ingredient and is not a drug.

paras: The ingredient is a palmitoylated tripeptide, with a fatty-acid chain attached to improve compatibility with skin lipids. Supplier information describes it as derived from sequences found in collagen VI and laminins and supplied in a water-soluble blend for use in emulsions [1].
It is distinct from other cosmetic peptides such as palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7, which have different sequences and claimed functions [1].

According to the supplier, the peptide signals the skin to increase synthesis of six components of the dermal-epidermal junction and extracellular matrix, with in vitro assays reporting large percentage increases in collagen I and hyaluronic acid [1]. These are manufacturer assay results and have not been independently reproduced in the sources reviewed.
A supplier-reported double-blind study in 25 women aged 42 to 70 applying a 2% cream for two months reported reductions in forehead wrinkle volume and depth versus placebo [1].

Independent studies include the ingredient only as one component of a formula. An open-label trial of a multi-ingredient anti-aging moisturizer in 37 women reported improvements in several skin parameters [2]. A serum combining vitamins C and E with a matrix-repair tripeptide was assessed with three-dimensional skin imaging and self-perception questionnaires in volunteers [3]. A face serum containing bakuchiol, palmitoyl tripeptide-38 and hydrolyzed hyaluronic acid was tested in vitro, in a patch test in 55 adults and in a human efficacy trial, reported as a preprint [4]. A completed 2025 registered trial examined an AI-personalized skincare regimen for photoaging in 43 women [5]. No trial isolating palmitoyl tripeptide-38 against a vehicle, run independently of the manufacturer, was identified.
The serum study in 55 volunteers reported no irritation or allergic contact dermatitis from its formula [4]. Long-term safety data specific to the peptide are limited.
The Matrixyl line received an in-cosmetics innovation award in 2015, according to the supplier [1]. The ingredient appears in serums, creams and make-up marketed for skin aging.

timeline.event: Patent application and claims substantiation documented, per the supplier [1].
